1.pericope_label: Behold, thou art fair, my love; behold, thou art fair; thou hast doves’ eyes within thy locks: thy hair is as a flock of goats, that appear from mount Gilead. Thy teeth are like a flock of sheep that are even shorn, which came up from the washing; whereof every one bear twins, and none is barren among them. Thy lips are like a thread of scarlet, and thy speech is comely: thy temples are like a piece of a pomegranate within thy locks

schools.summary: Henry gives the praise three purposes and denies that it is flattery or an invitation to pride: it is meant to encourage her under her present dejections, since whatever others thought she was amiable in his eyes; to teach her what to value herself upon, not external advantages but the comeliness of grace he had put upon her; and to invite others to think well of her and join themselves to her. All the beauty of the saints, he adds, is derived from him, so that they shine by reflecting his light and the spouse shines in her husband’s rays, and he takes the repetition to mark both the certainty of the thing and the pleasure he takes in saying it.

Gill notes that the words repeat an earlier commendation and are brought back to show that Christ’s esteem for the church was unchanged by all that had passed between; on the teeth he reports an old physician’s observation that human teeth resemble a sheep’s in figure, order and structure, holds the whiteness chiefly intended, for which teeth are elsewhere compared to marble, and prefers the ministers of the Gospel to the Targum’s priests and Levites, teeth being firm and sharp to prepare food for the stomach; on the lips he takes thin red lips for a mark of beauty and reads the words of the church in them, the scarlet marking the fervency of prayers and their acceptableness through the mediation of Christ.

Wesley adds a caution about method, that since the beauty is described part by part we need not labour much to fit each particular to some distinct grace, the design of the whole being to show the completeness the church has in part received and will more fully receive; he keeps to the facts of the place on the goats, whose hair there was of extraordinary length, softness and comeliness, in a country hilly and wooded and fit for breeding them, and says of the teeth only that the twins denote the two rows and that not one tooth is lacking. Clarke supplies the veil itself, a partial covering of black cloth made from the hair of an animal, probably the black goat, hung from the crown by silken cords ornamented according to the wearer’s means, leaving the forehead and eyes bare while covering the rest of the face and falling loose over the bosom, one such having lately been brought from Egypt and lying before him as he wrote; he adds that the clause within thy locks is not well translated either by our version or by the others, and reports the Latin sense as without that which lies hidden within. On the teeth he founds the comparison on the evenness, neatness and whiteness of newly shorn and newly washed sheep, and on the pomegranate he takes the figure from the cut side where the blush is finest, while allowing that the inside may be meant, finely streaked with red and white.

Ellicott holds that the derivation and the cognate Arabic words leave no doubt the word means veil, notes that the Greek understood it so in the one other place it occurs, and calls the rendering out of thy silence given here strange and meaningless, a defect the Latin mystified further into from that which lies hid within, which has been a fruitful source of moral allusion to the more hidden beauties of the soul. On the goats he reports a variety of contradictory interpretations of the verb, our version following the Greek, the margin resting on cognates meaning obtained or collected, the Latin giving which have ascended and the bulk of commentators the exact opposite, so that only the context can decide and any rendering suggesting dark hair flowing in masses round the shoulders is allowable; he adds that this author tends to accumulate and sometimes confuse his figures, so that the long soft black hair of the eastern goat is probably meant as much as the appearance of the whole flock on the mountain side. On the teeth he presses a Hebrew word meaning to make double, which may as well mean to occur in pairs as to bear twins, the second giving far better sense, since the rows are exactly paired, upper to lower, like sheep coming two and two from the washing. He also corrects speech to mouth from the parallelism and temples to cheeks behind the veil, quoting a Persian ode in which the pomegranate recalls the blushes of the beloved and an English poet on cheeks like apples which the sun hath rudded. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same result on the veil by grammar, refusing the reading that makes the word hair flowing down like a mane, since the preposition cannot be used of the eyes in relation to braids hanging before them, and deriving it from a verb meaning to stop up or to wrap oneself about, so that the veil is named as the thing which closely hides the face; they identify the scarlet as the worm-colour, the red juice of the cochineal, and argue that the word rendered speech is properly the mouth, the preformative being instrumental and the mouth named as the organ by which the soul expresses itself in word and manner of speech, for which the poet needed a fuller and more select word than the plain one.

debates: What does the word rendered locks mean? Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch both make it a veil, Ellicott from the derivation and the cognates and Keil and Delitzsch from the grammar of the preposition; Clarke reports that neither our version nor the old ones translate the clause well, and that one scholar denies the word ever means hair.

What do the goats do on the mountain? Ellicott finds the verb rendered contradictorily as ascend, come down, hang down or feed, and will accept any sense that suggests dark hair flowing round the shoulders.

Do the sheep bear twins or come in pairs? Ellicott prefers pairs, since the rows of teeth are exactly matched upper to lower; Wesley reads the twins as the two rows; Gill and Clarke keep to whiteness and evenness.
outliers: Clarke describes a veil of black goat’s hair, hung by silken cords and ornamented with gold and precious stones, one of which lay before him as he wrote.
Ellicott notes that the mistranslation out of thy silence, mystified further in the Latin, has been a fruitful source of moral allusion to the hidden beauties of the soul.
Keil and Delitzsch argue that the poet chose a fuller word for the mouth than the plain one, naming it as the organ by which the soul expresses itself.
themes: a veil, not a lock of hair

4.pericope_label: Thy neck is like the tower of David builded for an armoury, whereon there hang a thousand bucklers, all shields of mighty men. Thy two breasts are like two young roes that are twins, which feed among the lilies. Until the day break, and the shadows flee away, I will get me to the mountain of myrrh, and to the hill of frankincense. Thou art all fair, my love; there is no spot in thee

schools.summary: Gill allows the tower to be either the stronghold of Zion or one built as an armoury, quotes a traveller who saw its ruins standing aloft at the utmost angle of a mountain, and derives the word for armoury from a root meaning to teach, refusing the readings that make it a pattern for craftsmen or a lighthouse for travellers and taking it for the arsenal where young learners of the art of war laid up their weapons; he insists that the neck is likened to a tower not for height, an outstretched neck being a token of pride, but for being hung with spoils as a neck is hung with pearls and chains. On the next verse he argues from nature, that providence gave two breasts so that twins might each have a fountain of nourishment, and reads the young roes as marking smallness and the twins equality of size and shape. The sixth verse he gives to Christ and reads the daybreak as the day of grace rising on an elect sinner, with the shadows of ignorance and unbelief in flight; and the seventh he turns into doctrine, a completeness in Christ as to justification and, in sanctification, a perfection of parts though not of degrees, belonging to the weakest member of the church as much as the strongest.

Clarke notes that bucklers were often hung about towers both for ornament and for use, and offers a modern parallel in the pillars seen in armouries with weapons arranged on them in a great variety of shapes, such as anyone who has visited the armoury in the tower of London will have seen. On the breasts he refuses the game altogether, having met many attempts to justify the similitude and judging them unworthy of citation, holding that the poet speaks the language of nature, that language often fails an impassioned lover so that his comparisons come out without strict correctness, and that the description shows more of nature than of art, which he counts a high recommendation. He keeps the sixth verse literal, the morning breeze and the setting sun, and places the mountain among hills where the trees grew from which myrrh and incense were drawn. The seventh he glosses as every part of thee is beautiful, thou hast not a single defect, and sets beside it a Latin poet’s catalogue of a nymph’s beauties, which ends by believing the beauties yet unseen the best, together with an Indian poet’s praise of a woman in whom the beauties of a company of goddesses are collected. Wesley reads the tower as upright, firm and strong and adorned with chains of gold, takes the thousand for an indefinitely large number, and makes the neck the grace of faith by which the believer is joined to Christ as the body to the head; he notices that the words of the sixth verse were spoken by the bride earlier and are here returned by the bridegroom in answer, understands the hill of the church on earth, typified by the temple mount, and concludes that Christ is directing believers where they may find him, in his church and ordinances.

Ellicott doubts the tower can be identified at all, since even two towers minutely described by the ancient historian cannot be found and the structure known since the Crusades by that name is Herodian; the Greek version treats the disputed word as a proper name, rabbinical authority makes it a model for architects, and most modern commentators, differing over the etymology, still arrive at the sense our version gives, which the context seems to require. On the sixth verse he renders the clause until the day breathe, that is, when evening is come, and holds that the mountain of myrrh and the hill of frankincense are not to be identified, since they only carry the previous figure forward, the curtain falling here on the end of another day and on the union of bridegroom and bride. Keil and Delitzsch identify the tower with the tower of the flock, from which the king surveyed the flock of his people, and note that elsewhere it is called the tower lying out from the royal house, a government building on Zion used as a court of justice. They keep the next comparison to the figure, the pair likened for equality and youthful freshness and the bosom to a meadow of lilies on which the fawns feed, and observe that the praise stops there, so that counting the lips and mouth as one, seven things have been named, the eyes, hair, teeth, mouth, temples, neck and breasts, a sevenfold beauty. The sixth verse they give to the bride, holding that all who continue it as the king’s words lose themselves in absurdities, since they must then make the mountain and hill stand for her attractions and the figures would be grotesque; and they take her modest reply as what makes her lovelier still, reading the absence of blemish as covering soul and body alike, since the earlier verses praised her outward beauty while the sixth let her soul appear.

debates: Can the tower of David be located? Ellicott says not, since better-described towers have been lost and the structure now bearing the name is far later; Keil and Delitzsch identify it with the tower of the flock and a court of justice on Zion; Gill leaves it between the stronghold and an armoury.

Who speaks the sixth verse? Keil and Delitzsch give it to the bride and call the alternative absurd, since it would make the mountain of myrrh stand for her body; Gill and Wesley give it to Christ, Wesley noting that the bride had used the same words earlier.

How far should the similes be pressed? Clarke holds that language fails an impassioned lover and refuses to defend the comparison, praising the description as more of nature than of art; Gill defends it from natural history; Keil and Delitzsch count the figures and find a deliberate sevenfold pattern.
outliers: Clarke compares the shields on the tower with the weapon-pillars in a modern armoury, such as that in the tower of London.
Keil and Delitzsch count seven parts praised, the eyes, hair, teeth, mouth, temples, neck and breasts, and speak of the sevenfold beauty of the bride.
Ellicott reads the sixth verse as a curtain falling on the end of another day in the poem.
themes: a tower that cannot be found
a figure that fails on purpose
no blemish of soul or body

8.pericope_label: Come with me from Lebanon, my spouse, with me from Lebanon: look from the top of Amana, from the top of Shenir and Hermon, from the lions’ dens, from the mountains of the leopards

schools.summary: Henry counts the endearing titles, twice my spouse and three times my sister my spouse, and takes the change of address as marking a covenant, since the day of espousals was mentioned earlier and only after it is she called his spouse, his calling her so being what makes her so. He observes that no single relation among men is sufficient to set out that love, so that she is owned under two which among men are incompatible, a man who said of his wife that she was his sister having been understood to deny that she was his wife, whereas the church is both to Christ at once; and he draws from it that men ought so to love their wives as Christ loves the church, taking pleasure in it as if it were spotless when it is in fact compassed with infirmity.

Gill observes that spouse appears here for the first time, the day of espousals being past and the wedding garment on, and that the title is used chiefly to prevail on her to go with him, the repetition of the invitation showing earnestness and vehemency. He declines the literal mountain: it is not the range north of the land, famous for its odoriferous trees, but the temple built of its timber and the city that held it, which in Christ’s time had become a den of thieves and out of which he called his people; or else, the mountain being a pleasant one, it stands for the carnal and sensual pleasures from which Christ calls his people off. He also reports a rendering that turns the invitation into a promise, thou shalt come with me, the coming being the effect of a powerful grace and a drawing love.

Clarke thinks the word for spouse peculiar and reports the suggestion that a Jewish princess is meant, confirmed by the title sister as one of the same stock and country and so distinguished from an Egyptian bride, which is the ground of a theory that two queens appear in the song; he calls the opinion very probable while declining to contend for any system relative to this song. On the mountains he reports a commentator who finds an admirable poetic fiction, the beloved represented as a mountain nymph wholly occupied in hunting the lion and the leopard, a bold and undisciplined virgin unwilling to leave her wild and rural retreats, whom the king invites down from those hills with the promise of a crown, and adds that the classical poets described their huntress goddess in just those terms, quoting the lines. He then sets out the geography of the four summits named, one range dividing Phoenicia from Syria, another lying between Syria and Cilicia, and the remaining two beyond Jordan, south of Damascus and northward of the mountains of Gilead. Wesley takes the wildness as an argument rather than a picture, since the places where she was are not only barren but dangerous, being inhabited by lions and leopards, and the height is what allows her to see the place she is invited to.

Ellicott prefers the reading to me over with me, noting that the Greek and Latin read simply hither, a difference only of vowel points, and that the word rendered look has in the Greek its primitive meaning, come. He reads the verse as another reminiscence of the obstacles that had attended the union of the pair, the rocks and snows of the range that shut in the poet’s northern home and the wild beasts that haunted those regions standing for difficulty, so that like a modern poet’s shepherd, who holds that love is of the valleys, he calls her down from her inaccessible heights; to suppose a literal journey to these peaks one after another he calls absurd, since they are named as emblems of height and difficulty. He identifies one of the summits as a peak of the greater mountain and reports a conjecture about the other while saying nothing is certain. On the title he notes that the same Hebrew word is rendered daughter-in-law, bride or spouse according as the relationship is regarded from the side of the bridegroom’s parents or his own, and that its use does not by itself prove the pair were united in wedlock, since sister is joined to it in the next verse and it may be only a stronger term of endearment. Keil and Delitzsch reject the construction that makes the verse announce that instead of lonely mountainous regions and dangerous dens she shall now inhabit the royal palace with him, calling it plausible but unsupportable on three grounds, that the Hebrew would have to be built differently to say it, that she is not from that range or the mountains looking toward Damascus, and that such an answer would not meet her longing for lonely quietness.

debates: Is it come with me or come to me? Ellicott prefers to me, since the Greek and Latin read hither and the difference is only in the vowel points, and takes the word rendered look in its primitive sense of come; Gill reports a rendering that makes the clause a promise, thou shalt come with me.

Does the verse promise her a palace? Keil and Delitzsch reject that construction on three grounds, the shape of the Hebrew, the fact that she is not from that range, and its failure to answer her longing for quiet.

What are the mountains? Ellicott makes them emblems of height and difficulty and calls a literal journey absurd; Clarke maps them one by one and reports the reading that turns the bride into a mountain huntress; Gill takes the range figuratively for the temple and city, or for carnal pleasures.
outliers: Clarke reports a theory that two queens appear in the song, a Jewish princess and an Egyptian bride, and calls it probable while contending for no system.
Ellicott compares a modern poet’s shepherd, who holds that love is of the valleys, and hears the same call down from the heights here.
Henry notes that the two relations claimed at once, sister and spouse, are incompatible among men, and infers that the language must be understood spiritually.
themes: two vowel points and a direction
a bride imagined as a huntress
a mountain read as a temple

9.pericope_label: Thou hast ravished my heart, my sister, my spouse; thou hast ravished my heart with one of thine eyes, with one chain of thy neck. How fair is thy love, my sister, my spouse! how much better is thy love than wine! and the smell of thine ointments than all spices! Thy lips, O my spouse, drop as the honeycomb: honey and milk are under thy tongue; and the smell of thy garments is like the smell of Lebanon. A garden inclosed is my sister, my spouse; a spring shut up, a fountain sealed

schools.summary: Gill notes that the same person might be both sister and spouse among the Hebrews, so that the phrase is not improper in a love poem, while the church is Christ’s sister on the further grounds of his incarnation and her adoption; he adds that the word rendered ravished is a single Hebrew word found nowhere else and variously translated, the Latin giving thou hast wounded my heart. He applies the honey to the church’s speech in prayer, in praise, in the ministration of the Gospel and in common conversation, and presses the manner of it, that the words should drop freely and without constraint, gradually and at proper seasons, and continually. On the garden he reports two candidates, a narrow rocky valley below certain pools which the friars point out, and, more probably in his view, the king’s garden near the city, which was shut up and kept for the king’s own use and pleasure; the church answers to it in being marked off from the world’s wide waste by sovereign grace, in its smallness by comparison, and in its pleasantness and fruitfulness.

Clarke glosses the verb bluntly as thou hast hearted me, that is, taken away my heart, on the model of saying that a man has barked a tree or fleeced a flock. He defends the phrase about a single eye, which has been thought harsh and has attracted emendations, the margin’s at once having twenty manuscripts behind it, but judges the change unnecessary, since one glance is enough to say and the literal sense is good besides, the poet perhaps describing a look given in passing when only one eye could be seen; the chain he takes for the play of the muscles of the neck rather than a necklace or a ringlet. On the honey he supplies the classical parallel, that eloquence and persuasive speech were compared to honey and milk by the ancients, as in the epic where words sweeter than honey flow from the old counsellor’s tongue, and remarks that the figure is common to all writers and languages, an Indian poem having the like. On the garden he reaches the chastity metaphor by way of Greek custom and Greek poetry, since among the Athenians the women’s apartment was not only locked but sealed, as a comic poet complains, a tragedian praises a wife who had not broken her seal of conjugal faith, and another writer uses the phrase exactly as it stands here of a woman who had preserved her seal untouched; having established the plain sense he ends with an exclamation at how many will make metaphors out of metaphors. Wesley makes the doubled title the point, since the love cannot be sufficiently expressed by any one relation, reads the ointments as the gifts and graces of the Spirit, and keeps the garden practical, the enclosure being the care of providence and the shutting up a preservation from pollution, as springs were shut in countries where water was scarce and precious.

Ellicott reports that many give the verb of the ninth verse the exactly opposite sense to our version, thou hast emboldened me, and grants that the literal thou hast hearted me will bear either, the language of love approving equally stolen my heart and given me thine; but he thinks the mention of the neck-chain confirms the received rendering, the poet saying playfully that his heart was caught by the chain, and he compares a modern poet on rose lips and full-blown eyes that take the heart out of the breast. On the garden he says the closed garden and the sealed fountain appear to have been established metaphors for the pure and chaste wife, citing beside a passage in Proverbs a prayer still in use at Jewish marriages that no stranger may enter the sealed fountain. Keil and Delitzsch reject the emboldening sense by asking what is fitting, since the form can mean to make courageous and one old version keeps that, but it would be strange for a man who is no coward, and a king at that, to say that his love gives him heart, however well it might suit a warrior daring the uttermost to win a woman’s admiration; they observe that all the king calls his she can now call hers, since she has won his heart and with it himself. On the tenth verse they note that the two predicates praise her love first as it strikes the sight and then as it is known on nearer intercourse, and that praise of her person is intermingled with praise of the fragrance of her clothing, since her soul speaks not only by her lips but breathes out of her spices; the praise, they add, is sensuous but carries a moral consecration. On the garden they distinguish the words, the garden named from its enclosure, one term for the water denoting the bubbling wave and the other the place, as it were an eye of the earth, from which the spring gushes, and note that one reformer distinguished the two rightly while all the old translators rendered as though the same word stood in both places.

debates: Did she take his heart or give him courage? Ellicott reports both senses and settles for the received one on the strength of the neck-chain; Keil and Delitzsch reject the emboldening sense as unfitting in a king who is no coward; Clarke and Gill keep the taking away, Gill noting that the word occurs nowhere else.

Is the single eye a corruption? Clarke reports the marginal at once with twenty manuscripts behind it but judges the change unnecessary, since one glance says enough and a look given in passing shows only one eye.

What do the closed garden and sealed fountain mean? Ellicott and Clarke agree they are established metaphors for a chaste wife, Ellicott citing a Jewish marriage prayer and Clarke Greek custom and poetry; Gill and Wesley read the enclosure of the church and of providence.
outliers: Clarke notes that among the Athenians the women’s apartment was not only locked but sealed, and ends the note by exclaiming how many will make metaphors out of metaphors.
Keil and Delitzsch call the praise sensuous but hold that it carries a moral consecration.
Gill weighs two sites for the garden, a rocky valley shown by the friars and the king’s garden near the city, kept shut for the king’s own use.
themes: a garden marked off from the waste

13.pericope_label: Thy plants are an orchard of pomegranates, with pleasant fruits; camphire, with spikenard, spikenard and saffron; calamus and cinnamon, with all trees of frankincense; myrrh and aloes, with all the chief spices: a fountain of gardens, a well of living waters, and streams from Lebanon. Awake, O north wind; and come, thou south; blow upon my garden, that the spices thereof may flow out. Let my beloved come into his garden, and eat his pleasant fruits

schools.summary: Henry gives the fifteenth verse to the church in answer to the commendation, making it her acknowledgment that she depends on Christ to make the garden fruitful and owes him all the glory of it, being nothing without him: those who are gardens to Christ must acknowledge him a fountain to them. On the last verse he makes the church pray for the influences of the Spirit, who in his work upon the soul is as the wind, a north wind of conviction and a south wind of comfort, with graces in the soul answering to the spices in the garden; and he observes that we can invite Christ to nothing but what is his own already, and that the believer has no joy of the fruits unless they redound to Christ’s glory.

Gill takes the plants for members of the church, pleasant plants that shall never be plucked up, and notes that the word for orchard is generally thought Persic though one derives it from a root meaning to separate, the garden being enclosed. He derives the name of the saffron from an Arabic word for its yellow colour while noting that the Latin name comes from a mountain in Cilicia where it grew. The fifteenth verse he gives to the church rather than to Christ, reading the phrases in the vocative, so that on hearing herself commended she ascribes all to him and calls him the fountain of gardens and the well of living waters. On the winds he prefers to give the words to Christ, who has command of the winds and a property in the garden, since it would be strange for the church to ask for afflictive providences upon herself; but he reports the alternative that the north wind is being told to depart, it being spring, and raises two objections to the plain reading, that the verb blow is singular and construed only with the south wind, and that opposite winds cannot blow together in the same horizon.

Clarke takes the plants for the fecundity of the bride, a prediction on one view of her identity and a statement of what had already happened on another, and says the remaining expressions seem to refer wholly to matters of a connubial nature; he notes that the word rendered orchard is the one from which paradise comes. On the fountain he suggests it may mean one abundant enough to supply many gardens, and reports a conjecture that the word for gardens originally read lives. On the winds he reports that the south wind there is extremely hot and troublesome in summer and passes on a proposal that the verb we render come means rather enter thy repositories, so that the line should read arise thou north wind and retire thou south, the beloved being then invited into his garden by the coolness and fragrancy of the air; others, he adds, think winds from every quarter are wanted to carry the fragrance through the land. He ends by complaining that commentators take a literal sense where the metaphor is evident and at other times build an allegory upon a metaphor. Wesley reads the plants as believers planted in the church, pleasant to the eye and delicious to the taste, signifying the variety and excellency of the gifts and graces in the several members; he keeps the church the fountain of the fifteenth verse, since her being shut up does not mean she keeps her waters to herself, the church conveying to particular believers the waters of life she receives from Christ; and he reads the winds as the several dispensations of God’s Spirit, explaining that the garden is called both hers and his because of the oneness between them.

Ellicott reports that some have thought the offspring of the marriage is meant by the plants, but holds that the poet is plainly describing the charms of his beloved by a new adaptation of the language of flowers, and adds that the pomegranate may have been an emblem of love, having been held sacred to a goddess. He identifies the spices at length: the saffron is a well-known bulb whose dried pistil and stigma make the spice; the calamus he leaves open, since there are many sweet grasses in India and the East and the usual identification is not to be implicitly accepted; the cinnamon probably covers two species, the rind being what is used, the plant belonging to the family of laurels and growing in Ceylon and on the Malabar coast to a height of twenty or thirty feet, with leaves scarlet when young and turning bright green, and white blossoms. On the last verse he hears the airs of love called to blow upon the garden so that its perfumes may flow out and the beloved no longer keep herself reserved and denied, compares a modern poet on woodbine spices wafted abroad when a breeze of morning moves, and holds that the closing clause should form a separate verse, being the reply in which the maiden yields. Keil and Delitzsch take the whole list of plants as a figure for every phenomenon and utterance of her personality, quote a commentator who wished he knew how to unlock it, since in the flower-language of love all these fruits must have had their beautiful interpretation, note that in old German poetry to break flowers meant to enjoy love and that most of the plants named are exotics, and explain the word for park as an old Persian one for an enclosure planted with foreign ornamental and fragrant growths. On the fountain they mark what has changed, since the earlier comparison turned on the collecting and sealing up and this one on the inner life and its outward activity, a well of living water being one in which what it distributes springs up from within, so that it is at once given to it and its own. On the winds they read the praise as proof of a love that seeks a response, before which she thinks herself unworthy and asks the preparation that blowing brings, and notice which wind is missing, the east being purposely left out because the idea of what is destructive attaches to it.

debates: What are the plants? Clarke takes them for the fecundity of the bride and reads the whole passage as connubial; Ellicott reports and rejects the reading that makes them offspring, holding that the poet describes her charms in the language of flowers; Gill and Wesley make them members of the church.

Who speaks the fifteenth verse? Gill and Henry give it to the church, Gill reading the phrases in the vocative so that she calls Christ the fountain; Wesley keeps her the fountain, flowing out to particular believers; Keil and Delitzsch stay with the figure and mark the shift from sealing up to outward activity.

Should both winds blow? Clarke passes on a proposal to read retire, thou south, since the south wind there is hot and troublesome; Gill objects that the verb is singular and that opposite winds cannot blow at once; Henry and Wesley take them as the dispensations of the Spirit, conviction and comfort.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch note that the east wind is purposely left out, the idea of what is destructive being attached to it.
Keil and Delitzsch report that in old German poetry to break flowers meant to enjoy love, and quote a commentator who wished he could unlock the flower-language of this list.
Clarke ends by complaining that commentators take a literal sense where the metaphor is evident, and elsewhere build an allegory upon a metaphor.
themes: plants read as charms or as children
a fountain that is given and owned
